                        Dividend Reinvestment Plan
                        The Company operates a Dividend Reinvestment Plan (the Plan) which allows eligible shareholders to elect to invest dividends in
                        ordinary shares which rank equally with the ordinary shares of the Company. The allocation of price for shares under the Plan will
                        be calculated as the average of the daily volume weighted average market price of all Fortescue shares traded on the Australian
                        Securities Exchange during the period of five trading days commencing on 4 September 2026.
                        The last date for receipt of applications to participate in or to cease or vary participation in the Plan is by 5:00pm (WST) on
                        3 September 2026. The Directors have determined that no discount shall apply to the allocation price and the Plan will not be
                        underwritten. Shares to be allocated under the Plan will be acquired on market and transferred to participants on 29 September 2026.
                        A broker will be engaged to assist in this process.
                        A copy of the Plan Rules is available at www.fortescue.com/investors.

                        Net tangible asset backing
                        Net tangible asset backing per ordinary shares: US$6.35 (previous corresponding period: US$6.31).

                        The previous corresponding period is the 12 months ended 30 June 2025.

                         Real Zero
                         Fortescue advocates for businesses to adopt a “Real Zero” approach to reducing
                         their emissions instead of “Net Zero”. Put simply, this means eliminating the
                         use of fossil fuels and not relying on offsets (unless required to do so by law), or
                         carbon capture and storage.

                        OUR BOARD
                        Fortescue has a talented and diverse Board committed to
                        enhancing and protecting the interests of shareholders and
                        other stakeholders and fulfilling a strong governance role

                        As at 30 June 2026, the Board had 10 non-executive directors and two executive
                        directors, being Dr Andrew Forrest AO, Fortescue’s Executive Chairman, and Elizabeth
                        Gaines. Elizabeth Gaines resigned on 30 June 2026 and the Board will appoint Sigrid
                        Kaag as a Non-Executive Director subject to the completion of regulatory requirements.

                        Group Financial
                        Performance
                        In FY26, Fortescue delivered an Underlying net profit after tax attributable to equity holders
                        of the Company of US$3,468 million and Underlying earnings per share of 113 US cents.
                        The annual financial results were largely driven by the Metals segment and its performance during the period. Revenue
                        reflected record year shipments, increased price realisation and a higher Platts CFR Index during the period. There
                        continued to be strong demand for Fortescue’s products with Hematite realised price of US$91/dry metric tonne (dmt)
                        (FY25: US$85/dmt). Underlying EBITDA was also impacted by higher Hematite C1 unit cost of US$18.74/wmt (FY25:
                        US$17.99/wmt).
                        Financial performance for the year was also impacted by a number of one-off adjustments to the carrying values of
                        Energy projects including the Gladstone Electrolyser Manufacturing Centre, Arizona Hydrogen Project, Fortescue




For personal use only
                        Zero manufacturing and Metals sustaining capital. Additionally, pre-tax impairment expense of US$750 million and
                        Yindjibarndi legal compensation expense of US$104 million was recognised during the year. This is discussed further
                        under the Group Underlying EBITDA section of this report on pages 41 to 42.

                        SEGMENT REPORTING
                        Fortescue’s chief operating decision-makers are the Chief Executive Officer Metals and Operations and the Chief
                        Executive Officer Growth and Energy. Each of these roles oversees functional areas that may relate to the Metals
                        business, the Energy business or both. Notwithstanding this, the Chief Executive Officers assess performance and
                        make decisions about the allocation of resources for the benefit of the Group’s two operating segments identified:
                        • Metals: Exploration, development, production, processing, sale and transportation of iron ore, the exploration for
                          other minerals and decarbonisation of metals operations.
                        • Energy: Undertaking activities in the research and development of technology for industrial decarbonisation.
                        Corporate includes cash, intercompany loans which eliminate at consolidation, debt and tax balances which are
                        managed at a Group level, together with other corporate activities. Corporate is not considered to be an operating
                        segment and includes activities that are not allocated to other operating segments.

                        are eliminated on consolidation and are not considered material.

                        Hematite
                        Hematite C1 unit costs averaged US$18.74/wmt for the year, four per cent higher compared to the previous
                        corresponding period (FY25: US$17.99/wmt). The increase in C1 unit costs reflects higher diesel costs, unfavourable
                        foreign exchange impact from a strengthening AUD against USD to 0.68 (FY25: 0.65), lower mining and processing
                        volumes in FY26 partially offset by higher railed, shipping and sold volumes. The strip ratio increased during the year to
                        1.62x from 1.55x in FY25 reflecting higher overburden removed and lower ore mined.
                        While Fortescue has actively managed cost increases and supply risks throughout the cycle, the Middle East conflict
                        has impacted production costs in FY26, most observably with elevated diesel costs. A substantial portion of production
                        cost increases have been deferred into iron ore stockpiles and will be realised in future periods resulting in higher cost of
                        good sold in the coming financial year. Cost management will continue to be a focus, however inflationary pressures and
                        impacts of the Middle East conflict remain a feature in production costs.
                        Shipping costs have increased from US$1,432 million in FY25 to US$1,701 million in FY26, reflecting elevated shipping
                        market rates driven by broader volatility in global shipping markets and geopolitical disruptions during the financial year.
                        To meet Fortescue's shipping commitments, Fortescue employs a mix of shipping options which includes the use of
                        Fortescue-owned VLOCs, chartering third-party vessels and Free on Board shipments.




                                                                             FORTESCUE FY26 ANNUAL REPORT | 39
                        operating and financial review




                        Group financial performance




                        Magnetite
                        Magnetite C1 unit costs averaged US$105.37/wmt for the year, 13 per cent lower compared to the previous
                        corresponding period (FY25: US$121.21/wmt). The decrease in C1 unit costs reflects continued focus on performance
                        and productivity in FY26 and higher volumes sold, partially offset by higher diesel costs and unfavourable exchange
                        rate impact. The strip ratio remained relatively consistent at 0.47x from 0.44x in FY25.
                        Shipping costs have increased from US$37 million in FY25 to US$71 million in FY26 driven largely by higher volumes of
                        Magnetite ore shipped during the year from 7.1 million tonnes (Fortescue share: 4.9 million tonnes) in FY25 to 9.0 million
                        tonnes in FY26 (Fortescue share: 6.2 million tonnes). Shipping costs also reflect elevated shipping market rates driven
                        by broader volatility in global shipping markets and geopolitical disruptions.
                        Higher volumes sold and shipped were a result of improved OPF performance, enabling higher production rates. While
                        OPF performance has been hindered by reliability issues (low water availability to feed the plant), continued efforts




For personal use only
                        during the year to address these issues saw improved availability and increased production in FY26.


                        Administration and research expenses
                        Administration expenditure for the Metals segment increased by 55 per cent to US$372 million from US$240 million
                        in FY25. Administration expenses include labour, materials and consumable costs in addition to corporate shared
                        services and overhead recharges.
                        Research expenditure for the Metals segment has increased during the year from US$68 million in FY25 to US$159
                        million in FY26. In FY26, research expenditure related to decarbonisation activities including Fortescue's Pilbara
                        Decarbonisation Program, green iron, innovation and artificial intelligence.



                        ENERGY

                        Revenue
                        Energy segment revenue predominantly related to revenue from Fortescue Zero's motorsport and cleantech solutions
                        and newly acquired subsidiary Nabrawind's sale of wind turbine components. Energy segment revenue has increased
                        by 68 per cent to US$136 million in FY26 from US$81 million in FY25.


                        Cost of Sales
                        Cost of sales for the Energy segment is largely attributable to labour, materials and other costs incurred in delivering
                        Fortescue Zero and Nabrawind's revenue generating activities. Cost of sales in the Energy segment for FY26 was
                        US$138 million, which is a decrease from US$143 million in FY25.


                        Administration and research expenses
                        Administration expenditure for the Energy segment increased by seven per cent at US$207 million from US$193 million
                        in FY25. Administration expenses include labour, materials and consumable costs in addition to corporate shared
                        services and overhead recharges. Certain ongoing costs previously qualifying as research in prior periods have been
                        reclassified to Administration following the deferral of the green energy project pipeline.
                        Research expenditure for the Energy segment has decreased significantly from US$483 million in FY25 to US$232
                        million in FY26 following strategic decisions taken on the green energy project pipeline in Q4 2025. In FY26, research
                        expenditure related to Fortescue Zero's decarbonisation initiatives and electromobility as well as other energy
                        projects.

                        Depreciation, interest and tax
                        Depreciation and amortisation of US$2,872 million is up 15 per cent (FY25: US$2,506 million) reflecting a higher
                        depreciation expense than FY25 but in line with H1 FY26. The increase in depreciation expense in FY26 is largely a
                        result of:
                        • Increases in sustaining capital spend across various mine sites and infrastructure in line with the lifecycle of the
                          operations
                        • Increases in sustaining fleet and machinery including fleet replacement and components
                        • Changes to asset useful lives including assets within the Energy segment
                        • Commissioning of decarbonisation assets and transition to operations for key power generating assets such as
                          transmission infrastructure.
                        Net interest expenses have decreased by US$31 million to US$166 million for FY26 ( FY25: US$197 million) driven by




For personal use only
                        savings in interest expense from lower cost borrowings such as the Renminbi (RMB)-denominated syndicated term
                        loan and secured VLOC term loan.
                        Income tax expense for FY26 was US$1,477 million, representing a global effective tax rate of 34.1 per cent (FY25:
                        US$1,624 million, effective tax rate of 32.5 per cent). The effective tax rate exceeded the Australian corporate tax rate
                        of 30 per cent primarily due to the tax impact of overseas jurisdictions and non-deductible expenditure. The Australian
                        group’s effective tax rate was 30.3 per cent.


                        Exploration, development and other
                        During the year, Fortescue made one-off adjustments to the carrying values of Energy and Metals projects and assets,
                        with items of significance discussed below:
                        • Gladstone Electrolyser Manufacturing Centre: Following the write down of the PEM50 project and the Gladstone
                          electrolyser facility automation line in FY25, further developments in FY26 resulted in an additional write down of land,
                          buildings, plant and equipment
                        • Arizona Hydrogen Project: Following the write down of initial development costs in FY25, further assessments
                          were conducted in FY26 resulting in a write down of acquired plant components as no further opportunities have
                          progressed at this stage
                        • Fortescue Zero manufacturing assets: Following the decision to move away from in-house manufacturing to focus
                          solely on research, development and design, Fortescue made adjustments to the carrying values of Fortescue Zero's
                          assets including assets associated with manufacturing in the United Kingdom
                        • Metals sustaining capital: A comprehensive review was performed over the sustaining capital within the Metals
                          segment resulting in the writedown of redundant property, plant and equipment.
                        Further to the above, there were additional adjustments including the capitalised value of surrendered tenements as
                        well as minor capital asset and investment writedowns.


                        Impairment expense
                        At 30 June 2026, a pre-tax impairment expense of US$750 million was recognised for the Iron Bridge Cash Generating
                        Unit (CGU) (post-tax US$525 million). The impairment expense reflects Fortescue's latest carrying value assessment,
                        taking into consideration the revised ramp up schedule and a range of production scenarios, including nameplate
                        capacity of 22Mt.


                        Legal compensation expense
                        As at 30 June 2026, Fortescue had fully provided A$150.4 million (US$103.6 million) as legal compensation to the
                        Yindjibarndi People given the certainty around the existence of a present obligation and a reliable estimate (FY25: nil).
                        For further information about this legal matter, refer to Note 13 Provisions in the financial statements.


                        Other comprehensive income
                        During the year, a net loss on fair value of investments of US$61 million was taken to equity (FY25: US$96 million).

                        Financial Position
                        and Capital
                        Management
                        Fortescue’s capital management framework is designed to maintain a strong and flexible balance sheet while
                        supporting sustainable shareholder returns and disciplined investment in the business. Capital is prioritised toward
                        maintaining safe, reliable and efficient operations, followed by commercially attractive growth, decarbonisation and
                        strategic opportunities. The Group actively manages liquidity, debt maturities and key credit metrics through changes
                        in commodity prices and periods of significant capital investment, with surplus capital returned to shareholders
                        principally through dividends in accordance with Fortescue’s dividend policy.

                        Debt
                        Fortescue’s debt is structured on low-cost investment grade terms. The debt capital structure allows optionality and
                        flexibility to fund future growth. Total debt as at 30 June 2026 was US$5,931 million, inclusive of US$629 million of
                        lease liabilities. Gross gearing at 30 June 2026 was 23 per cent (30 June 2025: 21 per cent) and net gearing was four per
                        cent (30 June 2025: five per cent).

                        Revolving credit facility
                        The US$1,025 million revolving credit facility with a maturity date of 28 July 2027, remained undrawn at 30 June
                        2026 and 30 June 2025. If drawn, interest accrues based on a variable rate linked to Secured Overnight Financing
                        Rate (SOFR) plus a fixed margin and is payable at the end of the interest period selected (either one, two, three or six
                        months), with the principal due at maturity.

                        Syndicated term loan
                        On 16 September 2025, the principal outstanding on the syndicated term loan facility amounting to US$959 million
                        was fully repaid ahead of maturity date of June 2028, resulting in a nil carrying value at 30 June 2026 (30 June 2025:
                        US$957 million). The loss on extinguishment of US$2 million was included in finance expenses in the consolidated
                        income statement.




                                                                              FORTESCUE FY26 ANNUAL REPORT | 44
                        Secured VLOC term loan
                        In December 2024, the Group obtained the secured loan to finance the purchase price of eight VLOCs. The secured
                        loan matures in December 2034, and as at 30 June 2026 had a carrying value of US$231 million (30 June 2025: US$258
                        million) with a coupon rate linked to SOFR plus a fixed margin. The principal is repayable in 40 equal consecutive
                        quarterly instalments, six of which had been paid as at 30 June 2026. The loan is secured by the vessels together with
                        their accompanying commercial arrangements.

                        Senior unsecured notes
                        On 21 October 2025, Fortescue completed a US$750 million tender offer of senior unsecured notes, resulting in partial
                        extinguishment of aggregate principal totalling US$500 million of the 2031 Notes and US$250 million of the 2030
                        Notes. The carrying value of the extinguished portion amounted to US$747 million which was settled on 22 October
                        2025 for a total consideration of US$752 million resulting in a net loss on early extinguishment of US$5 million and was
                        included in finance expenses in the consolidated income statement.
                        Senior unsecured notes and green senior unsecured notes (Green Bond) had a carrying value of US$2,870 million at
                        30 June 2026 (30 June 2025: US$3,620 million).

                        RMB syndicated term loan

                        September 2025 with principal repayment of 0.5 per cent every six months, in arrears, commencing 7 February 2027,
                        and as at 30 June 2026 had a carrying value of US$2,098 million (30 June 2025: nil).

                        June 2026, US$103 million had been drawn under the facility, at an interest rate of approximately 2 per cent per annum.

                        Capital expenditure throughout the period consisted of:
                        • Sustaining and hub development, including replacement fleet such as the purchase of Liebherr T 264 haul trucks and
                          excavators, sustaining capital on existing mine sites, port and rail infrastructure. Development spend was incurred on
                          port development, industrial autonomy and hubs
                        • Decarbonisation increases reflecting electrified fleet and infrastructure, renewable energy projects including solar and
                          wind farms, transmission infrastructure as well as battery energy storage systems
                        • Exploration and studies, including West Australian and international exploration with increasing drilling activities in
                          Gabon
                        • Other projects, including expenditure on the Christmas Creek Green Metal Project
                        • Energy and Energy Projects decreases reflecting lower levels of growth and technology development
                        • Acquisitions during the year including Alta Copper Corp and Nabrawind Technologies, S.L.

                         For the year ended 30 June 2026, Fortescue generated Underlying earnings of 113 US cents per share (FY25: 110 US

                         Share Buy-Back Scheme
                         In 2018, Fortescue announced the establishment of an on-market share buy-back scheme of up to A$500 million which
                         was extended in October 2020 for an unlimited duration. The maximum number of shares which can be bought back is
                         determined periodically by the Company’s 10/12 limit, being that a company cannot buy back more than 10 per cent of
                         its voting shares within the span of any twelve-month period.
                         Fortescue retains the option to undertake an on-market share buy-back. During FY26, Fortescue acquired none of its
                         own shares on market under the share buy-back scheme.

                                                         RISK AND

                                                         ENVIRONMENT
                                                               MATERIAL RISK EXPOSURES
                                                               Our risk culture emanates from our Values, builds on Fortescue’s
                                                               Code of Conduct and Integrity and is operationalised through
                                                               the Fortescue Risk Management Framework (FRMF). This
                                                               emphasises that management, employees and contractors are




For personal use only
                                                               collectively responsible for being aware of the risks related to
                                                               their activities at every level and are accountable for ensuring
                                                               those risks are effectively managed and transparently reported.
                                                               We operate in a dynamic business environment which presents
                                                               a range of uncertainties that have the potential to impact, both
                                                               positively and negatively, our corporate objectives. We take
                                                               risks for strategic reward in the pursuit of our strategy, in line
                                                               with the Board’s risk appetite, to sustainably grow the business.
                                                               Understanding the risks that can materially impact our strategic
                                                               objectives is essential to support informed business decisions
                                                               critical to protecting and enhancing shareholder value.
                                                               The material risks that have been identified by management
                                                               and the Board could substantially impact our ability to create
                                                               or preserve value for stakeholders over the short, medium or
                                                               long-term. These risks, individually or collectively, could threaten
                                                               our strategy, business model, future performance, solvency
                                                               or reputation. Over time these risks will continue to evolve,
                                                               as we progress our portfolio of sustainable energy and green
                                                               technology projects globally, and as we expand our mining
                                                               operations outside Australia.
                                                               The material risks identified by management and the Board that
                                                               have the potential to affect Fortescue’s financial outcomes and
                                                               performance are set out below. For further information on these
                                                               risks and the broader risk discussion, refer to section 4.5 of the
                                                               Corporate Governance Statement.

                        • Diluted mining models are validated by reconciliation against historical production.

                        • The Chichester Ore Reserve is inclusive of the Cloudbreak, Christmas Creek and Kutayi deposits.

                          available from various deposits to meet the product quality specifications.

                                                                                    FORTESCUE FY26 ANNUAL REPORT | 54
                        ORE RESERVES OPERATING PROPERTIES – MAGNETITE
                        The 2026 Ore Reserves for Magnetite are from the Iron Bridge project. Ore Reserves for the project total 1,112Mt at an
                        average adjusted mass recovery of 30.4% for a 67.3% Fe grade product. The Ore Reserves are quoted as of 30 June
                        2026, on a dry in-situ tonnes basis prior to processing.
                        The 2026 Ore Reserves estimate was prepared by Fortescue's Technical Services team based on the current resource
                        model using detailed information on mining, geotechnical and processing parameters and the latest cost assumptions,
                        aligned with the operations strategy.
                        The Ore Reserves estimate is reported using a cut-off of 17% adjusted mass recovery. The adjusted mass recovery was
                        derived from the Davis Tube Recovery (DTR) mass recovery by applying an adjustment based on recent process plant
                        performance and will be reviewed periodically as part of an internally established technical review process.
                        Within North Star, mining activity within 100m of the Pilbara Leaf Nosed Bat (PLnB) cave, is prohibited by the current
                        Stage 2 Ministerial Approval (Condition 10) until such time it can be demonstrated that ground disturbing activity in the
                        area maintains the viability of the population of PLnB. Primary environmental approvals for the Glacier Valley resource
                        are in progress and currently with State and Commonwealth regulators. At this stage, neither of the above is expected
                        to have a material impact on Ore Reserves as plans have been developed and action is underway to address each of the
                        points. As part of the mine scheduling process, appropriate access delays and spatial restrictions are applied to ore
                        inventory in the North Star mining pit and Glacier Valley mining area to model the timeframe required for approvals.




For personal use only
                        The Ore Reserves have been estimated from Measured and Indicated Mineral Resources from within the North Star,
                        Eastern Limb and Glacier Valley mining areas. All Magnetite Ore Reserves are classified as Probable Reserves as of 30
                        June 2026 and will be reviewed as the process plant ramps up to full production capacity. Reserves have been adjusted
                        for any depletion in the prior 12-month period.

                        MINERAL RESOURCES OPERATING PROPERTIES – MAGNETITE
                        Mineral Resources for magnetite operating properties, which comprise the North Star, Eastern Limb, Glacier Valley, West
                        Star and South Star deposits, are stated on a dry in-situ tonnage basis. The Mineral Resources, including mine stockpiles,
                        are quoted inclusive of Ore Reserves.
                        As of 30 June 2026, the total magnetite Mineral Resource is estimated to be 5,999Mt (from 6,008Mt in 2025) at an average
                        adjusted mass recovery of 23.4%, reported above a 9% mass recovery cut-off. The adjusted mass recovery was derived
                        from the DTR mass recovery by applying an adjustment based on recent process plant performance and will be reviewed
                        periodically as part of internally established technical review process.
                        All magnetite Mineral Resources are reported within a high revenue factor pit shell (approx. US$200/t) to constrain the
                        reportable resource to mineralisation that has reasonable prospects of eventual economic extraction by open-pit mining
                        and has been adjusted for depletion of mined tonnes. The pit shell used to constrain the June 2026 magnetite Mineral
                        Resource was updated using detailed information on mining, geotechnical and metallurgical processing parameters, along
                        with the latest cost assumptions, aligned with the proposed operations strategy. Where appropriate, heritage sites have
                        been excluded from the Mineral Resource.

                        CAÑARIACO COPPER MINERAL ESTIMATES
                        Fortescue is now the owner of the Cañariaco copper development project located in Northern Peru. The project
                        includes the Cañariaco Norte and the Cañariaco Sur deposits. The mineral estimates for the Cañariaco project are
                        qualifying foreign estimates as defined in Chapter 19 of the ASX Listing Rules. They are prepared in accordance
                        with NI 43-101 and CIM Definition Standards, and as such are not reported in accordance with the JORC Code. A
                        Competent Person has not yet completed sufficient work to classify the qualifying foreign estimate as Mineral
                        Resources in accordance with the JORC Code, and it is uncertain that following evaluation and further exploration
                        work that the qualifying foreign estimate will be able to be reported in accordance with the JORC Code.
                        The reliability of the information relating to the mineral estimates has been assessed based on it being reported by a
                        Qualified Person as defined in NI 43-101 and in accordance with NI 43-101 in the Technical Report dated 10 June 2024
                        and titled "NI 43-101 Technical Report on Preliminary Economic Assessment". Fortescue is not in possession of any
                        new information or data relating to the estimate that materially impacts the reliability of the estimates or the ability to
                        verify the estimates. The supporting information provided in the initial announcement continues to apply and has not
                        materially changed. Fortescue intends to conduct a work program including additional drilling within the next three
                        years to report the estimate in accordance with the JORC Code.
                        Contained copper in the estimates, reported above a copper cut-off grade of 0.10%, are estimated to be 1,126.6Mt at
                        0.38% Cu in the Measured and Indicated categories, and 890.4Mt at 0.25% Cu in the Inferred category. The mineral

                        CLIMATE-RELATED
                        RISKS AND
                        OPPORTUNITIES
                        This section describes the climate-related risks and opportunities that Fortescue has identified that could reasonably
                        be expected to affect Fortescue's cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital over the short, medium or long term.
                        The disclosures below are organised into three categories: physical risks, transition risks and transition opportunities.




For personal use only
                               PHYSICAL RISKS                             OPPORTUNITIES                              TRANSITION RISKS

                        For each material climate-related risk or opportunity, we describe the current and anticipated impacts, relevant time
                        horizons, affected financial statement areas, key management actions, quantification methodologies, vulnerability and
                        alignment metrics, where these can be reliably identified. The analysis reflects Fortescue’s current assessment based
                        on available data, scenario analysis and management judgement. However, the timing, scale and financial effects of
                        climate-related risks and opportunities remain uncertain and will continue to be refined as our data, methodologies
                        and reporting processes mature.


                        SHORT, MEDIUM AND LONG-TERM TIME HORIZONS
                        We apply defined time horizons - short, medium and long-term - in managing alignment between our financial planning,
                        strategic decision-making and climate-related risk assessments.
                        For the purposes of this report, climate-related risks and opportunities have been categorised as follows: short-term,
                        where they may materialise within the next two years; medium-term, where they may materialise within three to 10
                        years; and long-term, where they may materialise in 11 or more years.

                        Time period                      Link to planning horizons

                        Short-term     0 to 2 years      • Aligns with Fortescue’s two-year budget cycle.
                                                         • This horizon reflects near-term budgeting, forecasting, operational performance, cash
                                                           flow management, and capital allocation.
                        Medium-term    3 to 10 years     • Aligns with Fortescue’s 10-year budgeting and forecasting cycle.
                                                         • This horizon supports medium-term financial planning, portfolio and investment
                                                           decisions, operational resilience, and opportunities progression.
                        Long-term      11 to 30+ years   • Informed by Fortescue’s 20-year long-term forecasting and strategic outlook.
                                                         • This horizon supports long-term portfolio planning, asset strategy, and scaling of
                                                         opportunities.

                        MATERIALITY AND FINANCIAL IMPACTS
                        Fortescue assessed climate-related risks and opportunities by reference to financial materiality, consistent with the
                        principles applied in the preparation of the consolidated financial statements and Fortescue’s Risk Management
                        Framework. In assessing whether climate-related information could reasonably be expected to influence decisions
                        made by users of general purpose financial reports, Fortescue considered both quantitative and qualitative factors,
                        including the nature, magnitude, timing and uncertainty of potential financial impacts. These factors were considered
                        in the context of Fortescue’s current operations, as well as the potential effect on, and alignment with, its strategic
                        objectives and business resilience.
                        Fortescue applied quantitative thresholds to classify estimated annual recurring financial impacts as low for impacts
                        between US$100 million and US$500 million, medium for impacts between US$500 million and US$1 billion, and high
                        for impacts greater than US$1 billion. The reported timing reflects management’s estimate of the applicable time
                        horizon in which the impact is expected to commence or occur. Quantification reflects management’s best estimate
                        based on currently available information, assumptions and judgements.


                        PHYSICAL RISKS
                        Physical climate-related risks arise from the direct or indirect impacts of acute weather events and longer-term




For personal use only
                        changes in climate conditions. For Fortescue, these risks are most relevant to our Pilbara iron ore operations and
                        export value chain, where the majority of our assets and operational activities are located. The physical risk identified
                        in this section relates to operational disruptions from climate-related events, including potential impacts on mining,
                        processing, rail and port operations, asset integrity, shipment volumes, operating costs and cash flows.


                        Our approach to physical climate-related risks
                        The Pilbara is already an extreme operating environment. As climate change is projected to alter the frequency and
                        severity of climate hazards beyond historical experience, understanding how these hazards may evolve over time
                        is important for assessing physical climate risk and operational resilience. To support this assessment, we have
                        developed climate hazard profiles that provide a consistent approach to evaluating physical climate risks across
                        different time horizons, including whether current asset design and operational processes remain adequate under
                        more severe climate conditions.


                        Climate hazards
                        A climate hazard is an extreme weather event or longer-term change in climate conditions that may affect people,
                        assets, operations or ecosystems. Risk arises where people, assets or operations are exposed and vulnerable to that
                        hazard.

                        PHYSICAL RISK

                        Operational disruptions due to climate-related events

                        Description
                        Fortescue faces a risk that acute weather events and longer-term changes in climate conditions will disrupt operations,
                        damage infrastructure and affect supply chain continuity across its Pilbara iron ore operations and export value chain.

                        Current and anticipated impacts
                                                                                                                                    Time horizon
                        Climate-related physical risks may result in temporary disruptions to mining, processing, rail and
                        port operations across Fortescue’s Pilbara value chain, reflecting exposure to severe weather events
                        as well as potential future changes in climatic patterns. Fortescue expects weather events to initiate
                        established emergency management procedures and operational controls, which may result in                       Short
                        temporary disruptions to production and/or shipments. Asset damage is possible. Damage to critical           0 to 2 years
                        assets, such as rail or port infrastructure, could have a significant operational impact. Events that
                        affect Fortescue’s ability to ship iron ore are expected to have the most significant financial impact
                        through reduced sales volumes and revenue. There is also potential for increased costs associated
                        with recovery activities, production inefficiencies across the value chain and remediation of damaged          Medium
                        assets at current replacement cost.                                                                          3 to 10 years
                        These risks are relevant across all time horizons. Over the short and medium term, impact is
                        expected to be within normal operating conditions. Current exposure is managed through
                        established controls and operational flexibility. Scenario analysis indicates that the frequency and

                        Key management actions
                        Operational assets are designed and maintained to operate in Pilbara conditions, including extreme heat and severe weather
                        events. Fortescue strengthens the resilience of critical infrastructure and operational assets through targeted investment in
                        asset integrity and redundancy.
                        Fortescue maintains operational continuity measures including continuous asset monitoring, response protocols, contingency
                        planning, inventory management and scheduling flexibility.
                        Fortescue is continuing to integrate physical climate risk considerations into strategic planning, risk management and
                        investment decision-making processes. This includes developing climate scenario methodologies, data capabilities and
                        assessment tools to support vulnerability assessments and adaptive planning over time.

                        TRANSITION RISK

                        Policy and regulatory uncertainty

                        Description
                        Evolving climate policy and regulatory frameworks may affect the cost, timing and competitiveness of Fortescue’s Pilbara iron
                        ore operations and export value chain. The impacts of this risk are most likely to arise through increasingly stringent domestic
                        carbon compliance requirements, fuel-related fiscal settings and emerging international maritime emissions regulation.

                        Current and anticipated impacts
                                                                                                                                     Time horizon
                        Fortescue’s exposure arises from existing and potential changes to climate-related policies and
                        regulations, including the Safeguard Mechanism (SGM), Diesel Fuel Tax Credit (DFTC) arrangements
                        and the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) emerging Net-Zero Framework (NZF). These                     Short
                        developments may increase operating costs over time through declining Safeguard Mechanism
                                                                                                                                      0 to 2 years
                        baselines, potential changes to fuel taxation settings and the introduction of maritime emissions
                        pricing mechanisms. Increasing market demand for Australian Carbon Credit Units (ACCUs) may
                        further increase carbon compliance costs.
                                                                                                                                        Medium
                        We monitor carbon markets in Asia and Europe, and, where appropriate, apply the market value of
                                                                                                                                      3 to 10 years
                        carbon in our investment analysis.
                        Over the medium to long term, financial impacts are expected to increase as climate-related
                        regulatory frameworks mature and become more stringent. The extent of these impacts will depend
                                                                                                                                          Long

                        FY26 impact: No material impact. Carbon compliance costs were US$9 million.

                        Financial Statement        Cost of sales; Other expenses; Cash; Property, plant and equipment; Cash flows from operating and
                        areas of impact:           investing activities

                        Key management actions
                        Fortescue integrates decarbonisation and climate-related regulatory considerations into strategic planning, capital allocation
                        and operational decision-making. Key actions focus on reducing exposure to evolving carbon compliance obligations while
                        supporting long-term operational competitiveness.
                        Fortescue is progressing its Pilbara Decarbonisation Program to advance its Real Zero Target through investment in renewable
                        generation, battery storage, integrated transmission infrastructure and the deployment of battery-electric fleets, charging
                        infrastructure and electrified plant. FY26 capital expenditure associated with these initiatives was approximately US$848
                        million. These investments assist in reducing exposure to future carbon compliance costs and fuel-related regulatory changes.
                        We also continue to assess and respond to maritime decarbonisation developments through initiatives such as Fortescue’s
                        investment in R&D to advance alternative shipping fuels. Fortescue also monitors policy developments and engages with
                        governments and industry bodies.

                        Quantification methodology
                                                                                                                                   Financial impact
                        Fortescue’s financial exposure is estimated using scenario-based cost modelling, current baselines
                        and independent price assumptions. Quantified impacts represent modelled exposures before future
                        mitigation or decarbonisation initiatives. These exposures are then considered alongside likelihood,
                        uncertainty and mitigation factors to determine the assessed financial impact.
                                                                                                                                       Low
                        Carbon compliance costs under the SGM are modelled using a business-as-usual emissions
                                                                                                                                US$100m to US$500m
                        trajectory, with carbon price assumptions applied to emissions above regulatory baselines. Two
                        scenarios are applied: a June 2026 spot price of US$27 per tCO₂-e and a long-term carbon price
                        of US$71 per tCO₂-e, expressed in real terms. These result in estimated costs of US$53 million and
                        US$142 million per annum, respectively, over the medium to long term.
                        Exposure to changes in the DFTC is estimated based on current diesel consumption at A$0.526
                        per litre, resulting in an estimated impact of approximately US$249 million per annum under a full

                        IMO Net-Zero Framework carbon levies. This indicates a potential impact of US$300-400 million
                        per annum by 2035, excluding any offsetting increases in CFR iron ore prices from higher maritime
                        transport costs.
                        Notwithstanding these modelled exposures, the overall financial impact is assessed as low.
                        This reflects that the above cost estimates represent potential outcomes before considering
                        the probability of those outcomes occurring, including uncertainty regarding the IMO Net-Zero                    High
                        Framework’s final design, implementation and how costs may be borne. It also reflects Fortescue’s               >US$1bn
                        active decarbonisation program, which will reduce exposure to fuel-related regulatory change over
                        time. Fortescue continues to monitor these developments and assess potential exposure.

                        TRANSITION RISK AND OPPORTUNITY

                        Market exposure
                        Description
                        Fortescue is exposed to a climate-related transition risk and opportunity as decarbonisation of the steel value chain may
                        influence demand for iron ore products through changes in customer preferences, product quality requirements, processing
                        performance and supply pathways that support lower-emissions steelmaking.
                        The transition also presents opportunities associated with increased steel demand and evolving technologies that support
                        lower-emissions steelmaking.

                        Current and anticipated impacts
                                                                                                                                       Time horizon
                        There is potential for both adverse and favourable impacts on price realisation, margins, market
                        access and competitiveness as iron ore demand is influenced by global steel demand, technological
                        change and decarbonisation across the steel value chain. Uncertainty in the timing and adoption of                 Short
                        lower-emissions steelmaking pathways may influence demand patterns, including product grade                     0 to 2 years
                        preferences and pricing dynamics, potentially affecting product mix and commercial strategy.
                        While short-term impacts are not expected, impacts may become more pronounced over the
                        medium to long term as transition-related changes in steelmaking and customer demand                              Medium
                        increasingly influence market conditions. Although changes in iron ore prices could materially affect           3 to 10 years
                        revenue, margins and operating cash flows, scenario analysis indicates outcomes are expected to

                        Financial Statement        Operating sales revenue; Cash; Property, plant and equipment; Cash flows from operating and
                        areas of impact            investing activities
                        Key management actions
                        Fortescue is responding through initiatives focused on product competitiveness, customer alignment and cost resilience.
                        Management actions include ongoing engagement with customers and the broader market to understand evolving demand
                        for iron ore grades, product quality requirements and inputs that support lower emissions in steelmaking.
                        Fortescue is also progressing initiatives intended to maintain product flexibility and support responsiveness to changing
                        market demand, including increased production from higher-grade supply sources such as Iron Bridge, together with ongoing
                        exploration, studies and resource development activities across the Pilbara and in Gabon.
                        To support resilience under a range of market conditions, Fortescue is maintaining a low-cost operating position in the Pilbara,
                        supported through operational efficiency, resource development and its Pilbara Decarbonisation Program.
                        In parallel, Fortescue is advancing Green Metal initiatives through studies, technology development and targeted investment
                        to support potential future demand for lower-emissions products and steelmaking pathways.

                        Quantification methodology
                                                                                                                                      Financial impact
                        This assessment has been undertaken using scenario analysis and price sensitivity modelling.
                        Independent transition scenarios, sourced from external providers, assess a range of market
                        outcomes based on differing assumptions for decarbonisation pathways, technology adoption and
                        infrastructure across the steel value chain.
                        Given the uncertainty and wide range of projected outcomes, Fortescue does not assign specific
                        forecasts or probabilities to medium- and long-term scenarios. Instead, the scenarios are used
                        to assess business resilience under a range of plausible market conditions. Financial impacts are
                        assessed through sensitivities to realised iron ore prices, with a US$5/dmt change in realised price                N/A
                        estimated to impact annual revenue by approximately US$917 million, based on annual shipments of
                        200Mt.
                        Estimated financial impacts are not disclosed due to uncertainty in long-term price projections,
                        reflected in differences across independent external forecasts and the range of external factors
                        influencing realised prices.

                        Fortescue has identified a material transition opportunity associated with the development and deployment of technologies

                        Key management actions
                        Fortescue is progressing its Pilbara Decarbonisation Program to advance its Real Zero Target. The program is integrated into
                        Fortescue’s strategic planning and capital allocation processes. Delivering a program of this scale requires an agile approach
                        to project execution to address the complexity associated with first-mover deployment. Key actions include targeted capital
                        investment in renewable generation, battery storage and an integrated transmission network; development and deployment
                        of battery-electric vehicle fleets, battery chargers and electrified plant; and development of Green Metal processing capability,
                        supported by dedicated delivery teams and governance processes.
                        Within the Energy segment, including Fortescue Zero, we are building capability and acquiring technology to accelerate
                        industrial decarbonisation. Fortescue Zero is focused on advanced power systems, battery management and intelligent
                        energy solutions. Fortescue is investing in next-generation renewable technologies, energy-efficiency solutions for hard-to-
                        abate sectors, and the identification and development of renewable energy opportunities at industrial scale in global markets,
                        including business opportunities to provide power to third parties.
                        Resourcing includes capital expenditure, specialist internal capability and partnerships with equipment manufacturers and
                        technology providers. Additional actions include engagement with suppliers, customers, governments and industry bodies to
                        support technology development and commercial scalability.

                        The global transition to a low-emissions economy is increasing demand for critical minerals used in electrification, renewable

                        the energy transition and may present growth opportunities for Fortescue.

                        Capital expenditure and climate-related investment
                        Capital expenditure is required to support Fortescue’s response to climate-related risks and opportunities and
                        to progress our broader strategic objectives associated with the energy transition. This includes investment in
                        decarbonisation initiatives towards meeting our Real Zero Target, as well as investment in Green Metal, critical
                        minerals, operational resilience and continued exploration.
                        Updates on climate-related capital deployment, investment priorities and associated funding requirements are
                        reported to management and the Board and are considered as part of our broader capital allocation framework,
                        financial planning processes and funding strategy.

                        Expenditure supporting asset resilience, operational continuity and climate resilience forms part of Fortescue’s
                        broader operating and capital expenditure. Fortescue also continues to invest in exploration, studies and resource
                        development activities to support the competitiveness of its iron ore portfolio and its ability to respond to evolving
                        market demand. Activities during the period included ongoing Pilbara exploration and advancement of the Belinga
                        Project in Gabon. These activities are driven by a range of strategic, operational and market factors, and the associated
                        expenditure cannot be reliably attributed solely to climate-related risks and opportunities.
                        In the short to medium term, capital deployment associated with the industrial decarbonisation and electrification
                        opportunity is expected to remain broadly consistent with existing guidance, including the previously announced
                        US$6.2 billion investment in the Pilbara Decarbonisation Program and the additional US$680 million to expand our
                        renewable assets, positioning Fortescue to pursue opportunities with potential demand for renewable power beyond
                        our own terrestrial operations.
                        Beyond currently committed and announced projects, future capital deployment will continue to evolve based
                        on market conditions, technology maturity, regulatory approvals, commercial readiness and strategic priorities.
                        Investment decisions consider resilience under a range of transition pathways and are not based on a single assumed
                        climate scenario.




                        carbon pricing
                        Fortescue applies carbon price assumptions, where relevant, in decision-making
                        processes including operating expenditure forecasting, long-term planning, investment
                        assessment and scenario analysis. The assumed price is currently based on a long-term
                        carbon price of A$97.92 per tCO₂-e, expressed in real terms. This assumption is currently
                        applied to Australian operations and investment activities. Activities in other jurisdictions
                        are assessed with reference to carbon pricing regulation developments in those markets.

                        Methodology
                        Fortescue considered the impact of transition-related changes in iron ore when assessing resilience to transition risks,
                        focusing on changes in iron ore prices under a range of scenarios, and the resulting impacts on cash generation, capital
                        management and target financial metrics such as gearing and debt to EBITDA.




For personal use only
                        Climate scenario analysis was undertaken in FY26 using Fortescue’s established corporate planning and financial
                        modelling framework, incorporating externally sourced third-party iron ore price assumptions for 1.5-1.8°C scenarios,
                        together with Fortescue’s internal assessment of expected product price realisation (“base case”) relevant to prices. The
                        results were assessed against target financial metrics while continuing with Fortescue’s strategic objectives over the
                        short, medium and long term.
                        In scoping the resilience assessment, a range of variables, including foreign exchange and inflation, were evaluated.
                        These variables were not included as explicit sensitivities because they are incorporated within Fortescue’s underlying
                        forecast assumptions and were assessed as secondary to commodity price impacts in determining climate-related
                        financial outcomes.

                        Key areas of uncertainty
                        All scenarios contain significant uncertainties relating to renewable energy deployment, technological development,
                        enabling policies and future iron ore grade requirements. The level of uncertainty is further amplified in the lower
                        warming (1.5°C) scenario due to the increased subjectivity in underlying assumptions. Within this scenario, a key area of
                        uncertainty is the extent to which global decarbonisation pathways will influence long-term demand for lower-grade iron
                        ore products.

                        Results
                        Fortescue’s performance over the past 10 years provides relevant context for the resilience assessment, including the
                        performance of its strategy through varying iron ore pricing and demand cycles.
                        Iron ore pricing inputs across scenarios and time horizons vary widely (Short US$85-$96, Medium US$65-$85, Long
                        US$58-$1112) however, they remain within historically experienced ranges. Based on the scenarios assessed, Fortescue’s
                        underlying strategy and business model have capacity to adapt to the transition risks modelled. Target financial metrics
                        were maintained across the short-, medium- and long-term horizons assessed. Where deviations were identified, the
                        assessment indicated that Fortescue has capital management levers, if required, that could be used to support continued
                        pursuit of its strategic objectives.
                        The assessment reinforced the importance of our existing monitoring activities focused on the pace of steel sector
                        decarbonisation, development of low-emissions ironmaking technologies, evolution of demand for higher-grade iron ore
                        products, and the long-term market positioning of lower-grade products under more ambitious transition pathways.
                        To support resilience under a range of market conditions, Fortescue is maintaining a low-cost operating position in
                        the Pilbara through operational efficiency, resource development and its Pilbara Decarbonisation Program. In parallel,
                        Fortescue is advancing Green Metal initiatives through studies, technology development and targeted investment to
                        support potential future demand for lower-emissions products and steelmaking pathways.
                        These priorities are reflected in Fortescue's strategic direction, including efforts to expand exposure to higher-grade iron
                        ore opportunities through exploration and hub development activities such as the Belinga Project, in Gabon, as well as
                        the acquisition of Alta Copper to diversify revenue streams.

                        RESILIENCE TO PHYSICAL RISKS
                        Fortescue is working to enhance operational resilience to help safeguard critical assets1 across its Pilbara operations
                        and value chain. As climate change is projected to alter the frequency and severity of extreme weather events beyond
                        historical experience, it is increasingly important to understand where existing measures may become less effective
                        under future climate conditions.
                        SSPs describe different plausible socioeconomic futures which, when combined with different greenhouse gas (GHG)
                        emissions and radiative forcing levels (e.g. SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, etc.), form scenarios used to assess potential future
                        climate conditions. They are developed by the international climate research community and presented and assessed
                        in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report (AR6).
                        We have engaged specialist climate data providers to produce site-specific hazard projections based on global
                        climate model simulations (Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6, CMIP6) for our selection of SSP
                        scenarios and time horizons. Further detail is provided in the Methodology section below and the Physical climate
                        scenario assumptions table.

                        Objective
                        Testing the resilience of Fortescue's strategy and business model to a changing climate




For personal use only
                                           Low warming scenario                                             High warming scenarios
                                              SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6                                              SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0
                           Time periods assessed                   Hazard types               Outputs assessed              Scope of assessment
                               Short (0-2 Years)         Tropical cyclone / wind, Sea    Operational downtime, Lost      Pilbara Iron Ore value chain
                                                           level rise & storm surge,              tonnes
                             Medium (3-10 Years)

                              Long (11-30 Years)            temperatures, Bushfire
                        Methodology
                        Physical climate resilience was assessed in FY26 using site-level modelling of acute climate-related hazards across critical
                        assets and operational processes. The modelling combined downscaled climate projections with asset design and operational
                        information to estimate potential impacts on operational downtime and production on an unmitigated basis.
                        For the short-term assessment, the model establishes present-day exposure by interpolating climate model simulations
                        between the historical baseline and early 21st-century projection periods. For the medium and long-term time horizons, we
                        assessed physical climate risks for 2030 and 2050, respectively.
                        Impacts from events of varying severity were weighted by their likelihood to estimate expected annual impacts. While severe
                        events may result in significant disruption, their contribution to expected annual impacts may be proportionally lower than
                        that of more frequent, less severe events. For example, a severe cyclone event that could cause three months of operational
                        downtime contributes approximately 0.5 days to expected annual downtime when assessed using an estimated annual
                        probability of 0.5 per cent (a 1-in-200-year event).
                        Fortescue has quantitatively assessed two higher-warming scenarios, comprising one intermediate emissions pathway (SSP2-
                        4.5) and one higher emissions pathway (SSP3-7.0). The use of intermediate and higher emissions pathways reflects uncertainty
                        regarding future emissions trajectories, policy effectiveness and climate system responses, with the high-emissions scenario
                        used to assess whether asset design standards remain adequate under progressively more severe conditions. Recent
                        observed warming trends and current policy settings remain broadly consistent with intermediate-to-high warming pathways.
                        SSP3-7.0 is used as the primary high emissions scenario across physical hazards because it represents an upper-bound
                        pathway that is consistent with the Australian Climate Service high‑end emissions framework. We use SSP3-7.0 for all hazards
                        except for ‘sea level rise & storm surge’ for which SSP5-8.5 is used due to the availability of hazard-specific downscaled data
                        and modelling.
                        Fortescue quantitatively assessed SSP1-2.6 as the low-warming scenario because it is supported by stronger model availability,
                        broader availability of Australian downscaled hazard datasets and greater consistency with climate datasets commonly used
                        for physical risk modelling.
                        Fortescue also considered SSP1-1.9 as the scenario most closely aligned with limiting global average temperature increases
                        to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. SSP1-1.9 was assessed qualitatively through a structured review comparing SSP1-1.9 and
                        SSP1-2.6 climate assumptions, warming outcomes and physical hazard implications to determine whether use of SSP1-2.6
                        would materially affect the outcomes of our lower global warming scenario analysis. The review found that SSP1-1.9 and SSP1-
                        2.6 are closely related low-emissions SSP1 pathways. The scenarios do not represent fundamentally different physical climate
                        futures for the purpose of Fortescue’s lower warming physical risk assessment. Accordingly, the use of SSP1-2.6 hazard data is
                        not expected to materially alter conclusions regarding resilience under a 1.5°C scenario.

                        Key areas of uncertainty
                        Physical climate risk modelling is inherently uncertain because future climate outcomes, hazard behaviour and asset-level
                        impacts cannot be predicted with precision. Modelled impacts are scenario-based estimates for the assessed time horizons
                        and are subject to uncertainty associated with climate system responses, including variability across emissions pathways,
                        climate models and regional downscaling approaches. Additional uncertainty arises from natural climate variability and
                        the potential for non-linear responses or tipping point behaviour within the climate system. Actual impacts may differ from
                        modelled estimates due to uncertainty in how climate hazards translate into operational impacts at specific assets and
                        processes. This is particularly relevant where multiple hazards occur concurrently or interact to create compounding impacts.


                                                                        FORTESCUE FY26 ANNUAL REPORT | 88
                            Results
                            Preliminary modelling indicates that, over the short and medium term, climate-related operational impacts are expected to
                            remain largely within the range of weather-related disruptions currently incorporated into mine planning assumptions.
                            The assessment did not identify a need for fundamental changes to Fortescue’s strategy given existing planning assumptions
                            and current response capability. Short-term operational flexibility is maintained through stockpile utilisation, production
                            sequencing and scheduling adjustments where required, which can help buffer the impact of weather-related downtime on
                            production and shipments.
                            The assessment did, however, reinforce the importance of incorporating physical climate risk considerations into long-term
                            resilience planning, including infrastructure design and strategic investment decisions. Under the high-emissions scenario,
                            and in the absence of mitigation and adaptation measures, modelling indicates that average annual effective downtime
                            could increase by approximately seven days in the long term relative to current conditions. Based on current production
                            assumptions, this equates to an indicative financial impact in the range of US$100–500 million per annum in the long term.
                            Fortescue continues to strengthen its approach to physical climate resilience by embedding climate scenario analysis and risk
                            assessment capabilities into business processes. These capabilities support the ongoing identification of vulnerabilities and
                            the development of adaptive responses over time.

                         Critical assets refer to Pilbara assets and supporting infrastructure considered essential to sustaining Fortescue’s core iron ore production and export

                        METRICS AND TARGETS
                        Fortescue is committed to profitably achieving our Real Zero Target by 2030.
                        We are implementing the key technologies, infrastructure and operational changes to reach this target, while maintaining mine
                        productivity and meeting our market guidance. Our focus is now on scaling these solutions and developing commercially viable
                        pathways for remaining sources of emissions.
                        As delivery of our Pilbara Decarbonisation Program accelerates to progress towards our Real Zero Target, Scope 1 and Scope 2
                        emissions are expected to begin declining from FY28 based on current plans and assumptions. The temporary increase before
                        then is primarily driven by three factors: increased ore shipped, increased gas consumption to meet growing power demand as
                        Iron Bridge ramps up production and increased total material movement required to meet current mine plans.
                        Like all businesses, delivery of Fortescue's voluntary emissions reduction targets is influenced by a range of technical, regulatory
                        and supply-chain factors. Achieving profitable pathways also requires that we continue to work closely with government to
                        remove disincentives to decarbonisation and support stronger emissions reduction outcomes.
                        In this context, profitable decarbonisation means that proposed solutions meet Fortescue’s investment requirements over the




For personal use only
                        relevant asset life, after considering capital costs, operating savings, and remaining life of mine.
                        The economic case for decarbonisation varies across Fortescue’s operations. At mines with shorter remaining lives, there may
                        be less time to recover investment, while some fixed infrastructure may have limited value once an asset closes. We manage
                        this by assessing projects against asset life, operating cost savings, deployment timing and opportunities to relocate or reuse
                        equipment and infrastructure across the Pilbara network.

                        In 2022, Fortescue set its three 2030 climate-related targets (described below) to eliminate fossil fuel risk, while

                        While our volume of iron ore shipped to our customers increased from 198.38Mt in FY25 to 201.33Mt in FY26, the
